title: Overview: Primitive Sequence Domination
content: Erdős Problem #892 (Erdős–Sárközy–Szemerédi 1968) asks for necessary and sufficient conditions on an increasing sequence $b_1<b_2<\cdots$ so that some *primitive* sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ (no $a_i \mid a_j$ for $i\neq j$) dominates it, $a_n \ll b_n$ for all $n$. The problem is open. Known necessary conditions come from convergence of $\sum 1/(b_n\log b_n)$ (Erdős 1935) and the sparser sum estimate of Erdős–Sárközy–Szemerédi (1967). This entry formalizes the 1935 necessity direction and exhibits a concrete non-example.
mathContext: Seek primitive $a$ with $a_n\ll b_n$. Necessary (Erdős 1935): $\sum_n 1/(b_n\log b_n) < \infty$; primitive $\Rightarrow \sum_n 1/(a_n\log a_n) < \infty$.

title: Primitive Sequence
content: Defines `IsPrimitive a` as $\forall i \neq j,\, a_i \nmid a_j$: the sequence forms an antichain in the divisibility partial order on $\mathbb{N}$. The primes are the canonical example: no prime divides another. More generally, squarefree numbers with the same number of prime factors form primitive sets. Primitive sets are necessarily infinite (any finite antichain can be extended).
mathContext: $\text{IsPrimitive}(a) \iff \forall i \neq j,\, a_i \nmid a_j$: antichain in $(\mathbb{N}, \mid)$

title: Strictly Increasing Sequence
content: Defines `IsStrictlyIncreasing a` as $i < j \implies a_i < a_j$. Combined with `IsPrimitive`, this ensures the sequence is both order-compatible and divisibility-incomparable. Any primitive set can be arranged in increasing order, so this is not a real restriction.

title: Sequence Domination
content: Defines `IsDominatedBy a b` as $\exists C > 0,\, \forall n,\, a_n \leq C \cdot b_n$. This is the Vinogradov notation $a \ll b$: the growth rate of $a$ is at most a constant multiple of $b$. The constant $C$ is existentially quantified, making this an asymptotic notion. Using $\mathbb{N}$ for $C$ (rather than $\mathbb{R}$) suffices since we can take $\lceil C \rceil$.
mathContext: $a \ll b \iff \exists C > 0,\, \forall n,\, a_n \leq C \cdot b_n$

title: Erdős Problem 892
content: Defines `ErdosProblem892 b`: given strictly increasing $b$, does there exist a strictly increasing, primitive $a$ with $a \ll b$? The problem is formulated as a Prop (rather than a characterization) — it asks for existence rather than stating conditions. The full problem would be a biconditional: $\text{ErdosProblem892}(b) \iff \text{some condition on } b$.

title: Erdős (1935) Necessary Condition
content: Axiomatizes `erdos_1935_necessary`: if a primitive $a$ exists with $a \ll b$, then $\sum 1/(b_n \log b_n) < \infty$. The proof: $a_n \leq C b_n$ implies $1/(b_n \log b_n) \leq C'/(a_n \log a_n)$, and Erdős proved $\sum 1/(a_n \log a_n)$ converges for any primitive $a$. The formalization uses partial sums bounded by a constant $S$, with an if-then-else guarding $b_n \geq 2$.

title: Erdős-Sárközy-Szemerédi (1967) Necessary Condition
content: Axiomatizes `ess_1967_necessary`: a stronger necessary condition. If a primitive dominator exists, then $\sum_{b_n < x} 1/b_n = o(\log x / \sqrt{\log\log x})$. This controls the growth rate of partial reciprocal sums, not just their convergence. The formalization uses $\varepsilon$-$X_0$ quantification: for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $X_0$ such that for $X \geq X_0$, the partial sum is bounded by $\varepsilon \cdot \log X / \sqrt{\log\log X}$.

title: GCD-Free Sequence
content: Defines `IsGCDFree b` as: for all distinct $i, j, k$, $\gcd(b_i, b_j) \neq b_k$. This prevents the sequence from containing 'divisibility obstructions' — triples where the gcd of two elements equals a third. For example, $\{6, 10, 15\}$ is not GCD-free since $\gcd(6, 10) = 2$ could equal another element. The condition is strictly weaker than primitivity.

title: GCD-Free Variant of Problem 892
content: Defines `ErdosProblem892GCDFree`: is `IsGCDFree b` a sufficient condition for the existence of a primitive dominator? This is a natural candidate for the 'sufficient' half of the characterization: if $b$ has no GCD obstructions, perhaps a primitive $a \ll b$ can always be found. The question is open.

title: Primitive Set Counting Bound
content: Axiomatizes `primitive_counting_bound`: a primitive sequence has $|\{a_k \leq N\}| \leq C \cdot N / \sqrt{\log N}$ elements up to $N$. This is optimal: the primes, the densest primitive set, satisfy $\pi(N) \sim N/\log N$, which is much smaller. The bound $N/\sqrt{\log N}$ applies to general primitive sets and follows from Behrend-type sieve arguments.
mathContext: $|\{a_k : a_k \leq N\}| \leq C \cdot \frac{N}{\sqrt{\log N}}$ for primitive $a$

title: Primitive Reciprocal-Log Convergence
content: Axiomatizes `primitive_reciprocal_log_convergent`: $\sum 1/(a_n \log a_n)$ converges for any primitive $a$ with $a_n \geq 2$. Erdős (1935) proved this using a clever double counting argument: the contribution of each prime $p$ to the sum is controlled by the fact that at most one element of a primitive set can be divisible by $p^k$ for each $k$. This is the foundational result from which all necessary conditions for Problem 892 follow.

title: Reciprocal-log comparison and the analytic inputs
content: The necessity proof hinges on transferring a divergent lower series to a contradiction. The multiplicative bound `product_log_comparison` and its `reciprocal_log_comparison` division form give $1/(b\log b)\le 2C/(a\log a)$ when $a\le C b$. Two analytic facts are taken as axioms: the Erdős (1935) convergence $\sum 1/(a_n\log a_n)<\infty$ for any primitive sequence, and the divergence $\sum 1/((n+2)\log(n+2)) = +\infty$ (Cauchy condensation). These bracket the comparison from both ends.
mathContext: If $a\le Cb$, $a,b\ge 2$, $b\ge C$: $\frac{1}{b\log b}\le\frac{2C}{a\log a}$. Axioms: $\sum\frac{1}{a_n\log a_n}<\infty$ (primitive); $\sum\frac{1}{(n+2)\log(n+2)}=\infty$.

title: The 1935 necessity theorem
content: `erdos_1935_necessary`: if a primitive sequence $a$ dominates $b$ (with $a_n\le C b_n$), then $\sum 1/(b_n\log b_n)$ converges. Proof: the primitive convergence of $\sum 1/(a_n\log a_n)$ pushes through the reciprocal-log comparison to bound $\sum 1/(b_n\log b_n)$ by a constant multiple, hence convergence. Contrapositive: any $b$ with divergent $\sum 1/(b_n\log b_n)$ admits *no* primitive dominator — the key obstruction.

title: GCD-free variant and a concrete non-example
content: The file records Erdős's GCD-free refinement (does a GCD-free $b$ necessarily admit a primitive dominator?) and a clean unconditional non-example: the linear sequence $b(n)=n+2$ has divergent $\sum 1/((n+2)\log(n+2))$, so by the 1935 necessity it has *no* primitive dominator. This concretely shows the necessary condition has teeth.
mathContext: $b(n)=n+2$: $\sum 1/(b_n\log b_n) = \sum 1/((n+2)\log(n+2)) = \infty$, so no primitive $a$ with $a_n\ll b_n$ exists.
